title: Bioluminescence: A Bright and Shiny Fish
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain bioluminescence, the production of light by living organisms through a chemical reaction between luciferin and luciferase, without heat unlike incandescent bulbs. They tour examples on land (fox fire, jack-o'-lantern mushroom, fireflies and their larvae, glow worms, bioluminescent sludge worms) and in the ocean's twilight (mesopelagic/dysphotic) zone, including the loosejaw fish's red light, dinoflagellates and the milky sea, and the cookie cutter shark. They cover functions such as mate attraction, prey lures like the anglerfish, camouflage via counterillumination, defense clouds from squid and shrimp, and the theory that bioluminescence evolved from an antioxidant process (coelenterazine). They also discuss a glowing cat made by the Mayo Clinic using jellyfish genes (fluorescence, not bioluminescence). The episode includes a long listener mail segment thanking listeners for gifts and cards, and a closing plug for the HowStuffWorks article.

segments.title: Opening banter and foot massage tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about a foot massage place on Buford Highway, fun spots, and fungus that may glow, then lead into the episode's bioluminescence topic.

segments.title: Incandescent bulbs vs. cold light
segments.summary: The hosts contrast incandescent bulbs, which give off heat, with bioluminescence, a chemical glow with no heat, comparing it to glow sticks. They mention Stone Mountain's laser show as a tangent.

segments.title: Bioluminescent life on land
segments.summary: Examples of land-based glowing organisms: fox fire fungus on rotting wood, the jack-o'-lantern mushroom, fireflies (lightning bugs) and their larvae, glow worms, and worms that give off a glowing sludge.

segments.title: The ocean twilight zone and blue-green light
segments.summary: The twilight zone (dysphotic or mesopelagic zone, around 662 feet deep) is where most ocean bioluminescence occurs. Blue-green light penetrates farthest, and most organisms produce light at matching wavelengths. The loosejaw fish can produce red light.

segments.title: Dinoflagellates and the milky sea
segments.summary: Dinoflagellates glow when disturbed, creating the milky sea visible from space. The hosts recall the Apollo 13 scene where glowing plankton guides a pilot to a carrier, and discuss the burglar alarm theory for why they glow.

segments.title: Why animals glow: communication, lures, camouflage, defense
segments.summary: Reasons for bioluminescence include mate attraction and signaling, finding food, lures such as the anglerfish, camouflage through counterillumination, the cookie cutter shark's glowing underside, and defensive glowing clouds from squid and shrimp.

segments.title: Chemistry: luciferin, luciferase, and evolution
segments.summary: Luciferin and luciferase react, often with oxygen and a trigger. The hosts discuss a theory that bioluminescence evolved as a byproduct of an antioxidant process involving coelenterazine, and that it arose independently in ocean species but not lakes. They also note the etymology of Lucifer as 'light bringer.' They mention a glowing cat made by the Mayo Clinic, which is fluorescent rather than bioluminescent.
